prompt: A server handling synchronous read requests is receiving 150% of its capacity. Results are useless to these callers after their deadlines. Which load-shedding practices are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Drop requests that have already waited in the queue longer than the client's timeout
options.explanation: Correct. The client has already given up, so processing them is pure waste. Dropping them frees capacity for requests that can still succeed.

options.text: Reject before doing expensive work such as parsing the body or querying the database
options.explanation: Correct. Shedding only protects capacity if rejecting is much cheaper than serving. Rejecting after the expensive part saves almost nothing.

options.text: Shed lower-priority traffic (e.g. batch, prefetch) before user-facing critical traffic
options.explanation: Correct. Criticality-based shedding, as Google uses, preserves the most important work when you can't serve everything.

options.text: Queue all excess requests in an unbounded in-memory queue so none are lost
options.explanation: Incorrect. Under sustained overload, an unbounded queue grows, increasing deadline misses and eventually exhausting memory. It postpones rejection while consuming resources.

workedExample:
Think in terms of **goodput**: requests completed successfully while their results are still useful to the caller.

The offered work exceeds capacity, so accepting everything cannot keep this workload healthy. Reject expired reads and shed excess work before expensive processing. Use trusted priorities to preserve critical work, and bound the queue and concurrency so admitted requests can finish. More queued work does not create processing capacity.

link.title: Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builders' Library)

prompt: After a traffic spike, a server's request queue holds about **2 seconds** of work, and clients time out after **1 second**. The server processes the queue first-in, first-out. Requests already queued are past their deadlines, results are useful only before those deadlines, and sustained new arrivals leave little spare capacity. What is the server's goodput, and what's the best fix?

options.text: Near zero until the backlog clears; drop expired work and bound admission so fresh requests have a chance to finish on time
options.explanation: Correct. FIFO spends capacity on expired work while new arrivals wait behind it. Deadline checks and bounded admission protect capacity for useful requests. Newest-first scheduling can help, but cannot guarantee a request will meet its deadline.

options.text: Normal goodput, because arrivals are back to normal
options.explanation: The backlog is still there. Every request now waits about 2 s, longer than the 1 s timeout, so its client has gone by the time it's served.

options.text: Near zero; the fix is a longer queue so no request is ever rejected
options.explanation: A longer queue means longer waits, so even more requests outlive their timeouts. Unbounded queueing is what caused this.

options.text: Half of normal, because half the queue is within the timeout
options.explanation: With FIFO, a new request waits behind the full 2 s backlog. None of them is within the timeout until the backlog shrinks below 1 s.

workedExample:
1. Already expired synchronous reads cannot produce a useful result for these callers.
2. Serving them consumes capacity while new arrivals wait behind the backlog.
3. Drop expired work using the propagated deadline and bound admission. Adaptive newest-first scheduling can favour still-useful work where the request semantics permit it.
4. Durable accepted jobs can have obligations after a client disconnects; the prompt deliberately concerns deadline-bound reads.

prompt: A backend cannot serve all offered work. Trusted critical requests fit within capacity, and some capacity remains for lower-priority prefetch jobs. With strict criticality-based shedding and equal-cost requests, which policy fits?

options.text: Reject the same fraction of both classes
options.explanation: Uniform shedding needlessly discards critical work that could fit.

options.text: Accept every prefetch job first so caches stay warm
options.explanation: That reverses the supplied priority order.

options.text: Reject all prefetch jobs even when spare capacity remains
options.explanation: Shedding need only remove excess work; lower-priority jobs can use remaining capacity.

options.text: Serve critical work first, then admit prefetch only into the remaining capacity
options.explanation: Correct. Protect the important class and use remaining resources without exceeding capacity.

workedExample: Confirm priorities come from trusted policy. Reserve capacity for critical work, then admit lower classes only while useful capacity remains. If critical work itself exceeds capacity, it too needs bounded admission. Reject cheaply and communicate retry guidance without promising capacity.
